Step-by-step verification of every numbered line (blank lines 0002, 0004, 0006, 0008, 0010, 0012, 0014, 0016, 0018, 0020, 0022 carry no content and are vacuously fine).

0001 - Framing sentence, no mathematical content; justified as an orienting remark.
0003 - Signature (constant e, unary f_0, f_1, binary P) matches the quoted book setup; the definition of C as the set of PCP yes-instances (existence of i_1..i_n with s_{i_1}...s_{i_n} = t_{i_1}...t_{i_n}) is the standard one. Minor imprecision: 'for some n in N' should require n >= 1, since the empty index sequence would trivially satisfy the equation; the intended reading n >= 1 is standard and is what the later argument uses, so this is harmless.
0005 - Correctly states the reduction obligation: from an instance c one must decide c in C via validity of phi(c). Justified.
0007 - The claim 'c in C iff phi(c) holds in every model interpreting sigma' is exactly the reduction statement needed (validity of phi(c)); justified. Note the answer will only discharge the left-to-right direction, which it announces explicitly at 0021.
0009 - phi(c) = phi_1 and phi_2 -> phi_3 reproduces the book's coarse structure; justified.
0011 - phi_1 as the conjunction over i of P(f_{s_i}(e), f_{t_i}(e)) matches the source verbatim; justified.
0013 - phi_2 as forall v,w (P(v,w) -> conjunction over i of P(f_{s_i}(v), f_{t_i}(w))) matches the source; justified.
0015 - phi_3 = exists z P(z,z) matches the source; justified.
0017 - The abbreviation f_s = f_{s_l} o ... o f_{s_1} for a bit string s = s_1...s_l is exactly the book's backwards coding, and it yields the composition law f_{s.s'} = f_{s'} o f_s that the induction at 0023 silently needs; justified. (Overloading the letter s_i for both PCP words and individual bits is a notational clash only.)
0019 - The intended reading of e, f_0, f_1 and of f_s(e) as the representation of the string s in the model is correct, and the observation that phi_1 and phi_2 FORCE P to contain all pairs (f_s(e), f_t(e)) arising from a common index sequence is correct (base case from phi_1, closure step from phi_2). Objection, non-fatal: the parenthetical 'which is what happens if M satisfies phi_1 and phi_2', and the biconditional 'c in C iff exists z P(z,z)' drawn from it, are literally false for arbitrary models - phi_1 and phi_2 only force the inclusion, not equality, so e.g. a one-point model (domain {a}, e = a, f_0 = f_1 = id, P = {(a,a)}) satisfies phi_1, phi_2 and exists z P(z,z) while c = ((0,1)) is a no-instance. The author himself hedges this in the same sentence ('perhaps in some other cases as well, but we wont care'), the line is explicitly flagged as intuition, and the remainder of the argument uses only the correct inclusion direction, so this over-statement does not propagate into any inferential step. It would matter only for the converse direction (validity implies c in C), which requires a minimal/term model and which this answer explicitly does not undertake.
0021 - Correct identification that the direction under discussion quantifies over ALL models interpreting sigma, whose domains may contain elements unrelated to strings, and that this is precisely why one needs a map from strings into the domain rather than assuming the domain consists of strings. The map s |-> f_s(e) is exactly the book's interpret (interpret(eps) = e^M, interpret(s0) = f_0^M(interpret(s)), interpret(s1) = f_1^M(interpret(s))), so the answer's paraphrase is faithful. Justified; 'correspondence' should be read as a function onto its image, since injectivity is neither claimed nor needed.
0023 - The conclusion is sound. Assuming M satisfies phi_1 and phi_2, an induction on n gives (f_{s_{i_1}...s_{i_n}}(e), f_{t_{i_1}...t_{i_n}}(e)) in P^M for every index sequence: phi_1 gives n = 1, and phi_2 with the composition law of 0017 gives the step. Hence if c is in C with a solution sequence making s = t, the pair (f_s(e), f_t(e)) is in P^M and equals (f_s(e), f_s(e)) because identical strings yield identical terms and hence identical elements, witnessing exists z P(z,z); so M satisfies phi_3 and therefore M satisfies phi_1 and phi_2 -> phi_3. Models failing the antecedent satisfy phi vacuously, so phi(c) is valid. The induction itself is asserted ('as we mentioned') rather than written out, which is a routine omission for an expository answer, not an unjustified leap.

Overall: every step that carries inferential weight is justified, and the argument correctly establishes the direction it sets out to establish (c in C implies phi(c) valid) while correctly explaining why the interpret function is needed for arbitrary models. The only defect is the hedged, explicitly intuitive over-statement inside 0019, which is not used anywhere downstream. Verdict VALID.
